title: India’s voter rolls, Microsoft’s outage: why software should bug you
shows: Abhijnan Rej, an Indian researcher and the founder of Tarqeq Research LLP, sets the revision beside a run of software outages in the United States in November, among them Microsoft's and a breakdown of the National Security Agency's internal communications. He writes that the opposition frames the revision as an exercise aimed at 'vote theft' and the disenfranchisement of Muslims, and that the accusations are undermined by the concern of Yogi Adityanath, the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, about its effects on Hindu voters and by senior BJP figures, among them the foreign minister and Delhi's Chief Minister, being flagged as discrepant cases in Delhi. In his reading the trouble points to glitchy and poorly designed software. He cites rules that he says apparently require a nine-month gap between siblings, which raise red flags for twins, and electoral software that accepted made-up voter names ahead of local elections in an Uttar Pradesh constituency in October. He argues that consumer software designed to look slick leaves most people seeing very little of how it works, and that such societies are fertile ground for conspiracy theories. He writes that the government has struggled to clear the air on possible problems in the Commission's software. He closes by calling for a wider public conversation about the trade-offs of large-scale digitisation.
quote: the SIR mess points to something more pedestrian: the use of extremely glitchy and poorly designed software.
A wider conversation around the trade-offs (and not simply the gains) involved in large-scale digitisation could go a long way in assuring the public.

title: The trouble with fighting political battles in court
shows: Kaleeswaram Raj, a lawyer in the Supreme Court, writes about the petition in which Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders sought the Supreme Court's leave to put 48 questions to the Commission as interrogatories in the case on the nationwide revision. He writes that the Commission answered with serious objections and objected even to the issue of notice, and that the case was adjourned to 9 December for a preliminary hearing. In his view the bloc was entitled to further details, because the Commission's counter-affidavit of 26 October, which asserted that its decisions on the revision were unanimous, lacks material particulars. He writes that with a report of disagreement from two election commissioners now public, the assertion of unanimity raises more questions than it answers. He recalls that the Court declined to interfere with the Bihar revision and in his account all but let it go ahead, and that West Bengal's revision met a similar result through a different mechanism. Drawing on Charles Taylor's warning that litigation turns political disputes into a zero-sum game, and on Indian and foreign cases, he argues that litigation is no substitute for mass movements and that protests should not be put off while a case is pending. He closes by agreeing with Rahul Gandhi that peaceful agitation will go on whatever the court decides, and grounds that in the freedoms of expression and association under Article 19.
quote: In a democracy, litigation is not a substitute for mass movements.
The postponement of a movement or a protest in light of a litigative process could be unwise.
